scenarios.title: Extract an inventory view
scenarios.summary: Select asset and owner fields without damaging spaces or empty values.
scenarios.objective: The argument names an existing inventory file. Records use asset:room:owner, with optional extra fields; lines without a colon are notes. Print fields 1 and 3, separated by a colon, in original record order. Skip notes, keep empty selected fields, ignore extra fields and print a newline after every selected record. If a later selected field is absent, print only selected fields that exist. Return 0, print no errors and leave every file unchanged. Supplied filenames never begin with a hyphen.

hints: Count fields from 1: asset, room, owner. A colon separates fields; spaces inside a field stay unchanged.
cut -f selects field numbers, -d chooses the delimiter, and -s skips lines with no delimiter.
A list such as 1,3 selects those fields in input order. It does not rearrange fields when you reverse the list.

# Select the asset and owner, excluding room and note lines.
cut -d : -f 2 "$1"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use quoted file arguments and pipelines from earlier units. This lesson introduces delimited fields and cut.

concepts.title: A record can contain several pieces
concepts.text: A line such as cable:Store:Jules has three fields: cable, Store and Jules. A field is one piece separated by the chosen character. Here colon is the separator; spaces inside a piece remain data.

concepts.title: Select fields instead of searching for text
concepts.text: cut -d : -f 1,3 prints fields 1 and 3 with the same separator. Numbering starts at 1. Add -s to skip lines with no separator. Selected fields stay in their original order, and a missing later field is simply absent.

concepts.title: Know which format you are reading
concepts.text: This is simple delimiter-separated text, not quoted CSV: a colon always separates fields. The example uses different items. Run it, change the selection and inspect the output; no input file changes.

teaching.inputs: labels.txt contains cable:Store:Jules, a note without colons, and plug:Lab:Nora, each on its own line.
teaching.try_change: Change 1,3 to 2,3 and run again. The location replaces the item in each output record.

fixture.name: Choose fields from a different list

scenarios.retry_guidance: If room names appear, check the field numbers. If notes remain, check -s. Empty owner fields should keep their separator; spaces are part of a field, not extra columns.
scenarios.explanation: cut selects existing fields in source order, preserves their text and uses the delimiter between selected fields. -s excludes note lines without a delimiter. Quoting the filename preserves spaces; it does not change the colon-based field format.

scenarios.objective: The argument names an existing file containing one nonempty entry per line, in arbitrary order. Print each distinct whole entry once, in ascending C/POSIX byte order. Keep case, spaces and percent signs unchanged; uppercase and lowercase are different. Treat numeric-looking names as text (10 sorts before 2). Add a newline to the final output entry even if the input lacked one. Return 0, print no errors and change no files. An empty input prints nothing; supplied filenames never begin with a hyphen.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use whole-line files and field extraction from the previous activity. This lesson introduces sorting and unique whole-line values.

concepts.title: Make the order predictable
concepts.text: sort reads lines and prints them in order. These labs use C/POSIX byte order: spaces and uppercase/lowercase matter. Numeric-looking labels remain text, so 10 comes before 2. This is not a promise about every human-language alphabet or locale.

concepts.title: Keep one copy of each identical line
concepts.text: sort -u combines sorting with removing identical lines, even when the original copies were far apart. It does not merge desk A with desk  A, because their spacing differs. The original file is left unchanged.

concepts.title: Print output or save it deliberately
concepts.text: The example prints its result. A > redirection would replace a destination file, as in the earlier report lessons. The assignment only needs printed output; do not edit or overwrite its input.

teaching.inputs: queue.txt contains plug, cable and plug, each followed by a newline.
teaching.try_change: Change -u to -r and run again. The queue reverses, and both plug lines remain.

scenarios.retry_guidance: If repeats remain, sort must also remove identical lines. If 2 precedes 10, the task calls for text order, not numeric sorting. Keep case and spacing exactly as supplied.
scenarios.explanation: Sorting complete lines keeps the list in a repeatable order without changing its names. -u removes identical sorted lines. An equivalent sort followed by adjacent deduplication also works; unsorted adjacent deduplication alone can miss separated copies.

scenarios.title: Count locations without losing repeats
scenarios.summary: Build a location summary from unsorted inventory records.
scenarios.objective: The argument names an existing file of location:asset records; every record contains a colon. Print a count of records for each distinct location, ordered by location in C/POSIX byte order. Keep case and spaces; an empty location is a real value to count. Use the GNU-style uniq -c format: a right-aligned seven-column count, one space, the location and a newline. Return 0, print no errors and leave all files unchanged. Empty input prints nothing; supplied filenames never begin with a hyphen.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use cut, whole-line sorting and pipelines from the previous two activities. This lesson introduces adjacent groups and uniq counts.

concepts.title: Adjacent means next to each other
concepts.text: uniq combines runs of identical neighboring lines. It does not remember a name that appeared much earlier. sort first when you want all copies of a location to become one neighboring group.

concepts.title: Count a group without removing its evidence
concepts.text: uniq -c prints how many input lines were in each group. The GNU-style count uses a seven-character-wide space-padded column followed by a space and the original value. Let the utility format it; no manual padding is needed. sort -u first would throw away the counts you need.

concepts.title: Transform records in useful stages
concepts.text: The assignment starts with location:asset records. cut selects locations, sort puts equal values together, and uniq -c counts them. The example already contains one item per line, so it needs only the final two stages.

teaching.inputs: queue.txt contains plug, cable, plug, cable, cable, on separate lines. No arguments or supplied variables.
teaching.try_change: Change -c to -d and run again. Repeated items are listed once, without counts.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Counts split into several entries for the same location mean identical lines were not made adjacent. Counts of 1 everywhere may mean -u removed duplicates before counting. Compare spaces and the empty-location group carefully.
scenarios.explanation: Extract fields before grouping so different asset names do not keep the same location apart. Sorting makes equal location lines adjacent. uniq -c counts every record in that group and provides consistent spacing; empty selected fields remain real empty lines.

scenarios.title: Audit duplicate asset identities
scenarios.summary: Combine field selection, grouping and safe report replacement into a data-quality audit.
scenarios.objective: Write an inventory audit. Exactly two arguments name an input file and output file. Data records have a nonempty asset ID before the first colon; lines without a colon are notes to skip. On success replace the output with Duplicate asset IDs plus a newline, then each ID appearing in at least two records once, in ascending C/POSIX byte order. Keep IDs case-sensitive and preserve spaces. Print Saved: OUTPUT plus a newline; return 0 with no errors. If the input is missing, the output-filename argument is empty/missing, argument count differs, or both names are identical, print only Cannot audit inventory plus a newline to standard error, return 2 and leave all files unchanged. Supplied filenames have no directory parts or leading hyphen; equality of these names is not general real-file alias protection.

initial.source:
# Arguments: an input inventory and an output audit filename.
input=$1
output=$2
# Check the arguments and input before changing any file.
# Build the audit heading and duplicate-ID list, then print confirmation.

files./work/source.txt:
rack  A:one
rack A:two
rack  A:three
10:x
2:y
10:z
note

after./work/source.txt:
rack  A:one
rack A:two
rack  A:three
10:x
2:y
10:z
note

cases.name: Missing source must not create output

solution:
if [ "$#" -ne 2 ] || [ -z "$2" ] || [ "$1" = "$2" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot audit inventory\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ -f "$1" ]; then
    :
else
    printf 'Cannot audit inventory\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
printf 'Duplicate asset IDs\n' > "$2"
cut -s -d : -f 1 "$1" | sort | uniq -d >> "$2"
printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$2"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combines the three text-processing lessons with validation, exit status and safe redirection from the earlier report capstone. This lesson adds argument-count and filename comparisons, plus uniq -d as the repeated-groups filter.

concepts.title: An identity collision can hide in different rows
concepts.text: If cable appears in both cable:Store and cable:Desk, the full lines differ but the ID is duplicated. Select the identity field before deciding what repeats. Note lines without a colon are not records in this deliberately simple format.

concepts.title: Select repeated groups
concepts.text: After sort makes equal IDs neighbors, uniq -d prints each group with two or more members once. uniq alone also prints singletons; sort -u removes the evidence of repetition. The small example finds repeated IDs without writing a report.

concepts.title: Protect data before publishing a report
concepts.text: Validate both arguments and the source before any > or >>. Then replace the report heading and append the duplicate list. Supplied names are canonical single filenames; real filesystem links/alternate paths require more than textual equality, outside this activity.

concepts.title: Check the count and compare names
concepts.text: The assignment requires exactly two arguments: [ "$#" -ne 2 ] succeeds when the supplied argument count is not two. -ne compares numbers; [ "$input" = "$output" ] compares text exactly. A || B tries B only if A fails; a guard joining invalid checks with || rejects when any check succeeds. The small example has no supplied arguments, so it creates count=2 and two filenames to practice these tests. In the assignment, use the real "$#", "$1" and "$2", and reject an empty output with -z, before any > or >>.

teaching.example:
count=2
input=labels.txt
output=example-audit.txt
if [ "$count" -ne 2 ] || [ "$input" = "$output" ]; then
    printf 'Choose two distinct example names\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
cut -s -d : -f 1 labels.txt | sort | uniq -d
teaching.inputs: No arguments are supplied. The script creates count, input and output as practice values; it does not write an output file. labels.txt contains cable:Store, plug:Lab, cable:Desk and note only, on separate lines.
teaching.try_change: Change count=2 to count=1 and Run: the guard prints only an error and exits 2 before filtering. Restore count=2, then change output=example-audit.txt to output=labels.txt to exercise the filename collision check. Restore the distinct name afterward.

scenarios.retry_guidance: If single-use IDs appear, the last stage is not repeated-only selection. If a repeated ID is missing, check that sorting happens before grouping. If invalid input changes files, move redirection after validation.
scenarios.explanation: The pipeline answers a different question at each stage: which ID is in this row, which equal IDs can be grouped, and which groups contain more than one row? A heading-only report is a valid success when no duplicates exist. Validation precedes replacement so a missing source cannot destroy the old audit. The comparison applies only to the supplied simple filenames, not every real alias or file format.
